_comment: The misconceptions Cambridge names for Stage 6, from the 'Common misconceptions' table in each topic of the Teacher's Resource. Same shape and same extraction method as the Stage 5 fixture beside it: Cambridge's own wording in `misconception` and `overcome`, plus an authored `learner` pair - [what many think, what is really true] - which is what the unit's 'Common misconceptions' panel shows the child.
source: Cambridge Primary Science Teacher's Resource 6 (Cambridge University Press), Common misconceptions tables. 12 topics carry one, 14 distinct rows.
_minimumCovered: The count with a `learner` pair and a unit to sit in. Coverage is a number that only goes up. It is 7 of 14 because Grade 6 has only five units and half of Cambridge's Stage 6 misconceptions belong to topics none of them covers - see _excluded.

_excluded._comment: Cambridge names these for Stage 6 and no Grade 6 unit could answer them. Recorded rather than dropped: the absence is the finding. Grade 6 has five units against a 59-objective stage, and the whole Earth-and-space strand plus the health-and-disease strand have no unit at all, which is why half of these have nowhere to go. One - the flotation row - was deliverable until an audit showed the forces unit does not teach flotation after all.
_excluded.Using antibacterial soaps and cleaning p: 6Bp.02-6Bp.04 (infection, hygiene, the body's defences). Grade 6 has no disease content: every hit for bacteria or fungi in the grade is a decomposer in the ecosystems unit, or the bacteria in yoghurt.
_excluded.Gases have no mass: 6Cp.02 (gases have properties, including mass), which no Grade 6 unit claims or teaches.
_excluded.The temperature of a boiling liquid incr: 6Cc.03 (the difference between boiling and evaporation). The materials unit says 'boiling water into steam' and never contrasts the two, so the objective is not claimed.
_excluded.If water is clear, it is safe to drink a: 6Be.02 (toxic substances moving through a food chain). No occurrence of toxic, toxin, poison or pesticide anywhere in Grade 6; the unit's 'Human Impact' concept is about habitat loss.
_excluded.Heavy objects sink and light objects flo: 6Pf.05 (mass and shape affecting whether an object floats). This row was going to be delivered until the claim behind it was audited: the only float/sink text in the forces unit is 'you do not sink through [the chair]' - a normal force - and 'the person floats down gently', a parachutist under air resistance. Neither is flotation, so 6Pf.05 was dropped and this row has nowhere to sit.
_excluded.Some surfaces such as wood do not reflec: 6Ps.01 (a ray of light reflected from a plane mirror). Grade 6 has no light unit; 0097 places reflection at Stage 4 and plane mirrors at Stage 6, and Grade 5 teaches the Stage 4 material instead.
_excluded.The Moon is only in the sky at night: 6ESs.01 and 6ESs.02 (the Solar System; the Moon's monthly cycle). Grade 6 has no space unit. Grade 5 Unit 6 teaches the Moon's phases. CORRECTED 2026-09-17: this said the row 'becomes deliverable by moving that concept rather than by authoring anything', and that is wrong. 0846 places The Earth and beyond at Stage 5 and gives Stage 6 no astronomy sub-strand at all, so Grade 6's five units are one per 0846 Stage 6 sub-strand and none is about space. The concept is where the old framework put it and has nowhere to move to.

misconceptions.misconception: Blood in the veins is blue, due to diagrams of the circulatory system showing the veins in blue.
misconceptions.overcome: Explain that the blood in both the arteries and veins is red but the blood in the veins is darker red as it carries very little oxygen. (The exception is the pulmonary veins from the lungs.)
learner: The blood in your veins is blue - that is why veins are drawn blue.
All of your blood is red. Blood in the veins is a darker red because it has given away most of its oxygen. Diagrams colour veins blue only to tell them apart from arteries.

misconceptions.misconception: Teachers often use a balloon to demonstrate how the lungs expand and contract during breathing. This practice may lead learners to think that the lungs are hollow organs like balloons that can fill up with air when we inhale and collapse and empty when we exhale.
misconceptions.overcome: Use a bath sponge to explain to learners that the lungs are not hollow but are spongy and made up of numerous tiny air sacs, like the bath sponge. If possible, show a slide or video clip of the lungs.
learner: Your lungs are hollow bags that fill up with air like balloons.

A lung is spongy, not hollow. It is packed with millions of tiny air sacs - far more like a bath sponge than a balloon - and all those sacs are what give the air enough surface to pass into your blood.

misconceptions.misconception: Food chain arrows represent who eats whom rather than flow of energy.
misconceptions.overcome: Explain that living things eat other living things in order to get the energy they need to live. A food chain is a drawing that shows the order in which energy passes from one living thing to another in the food it eats.
learner: The arrows in a food chain show who eats whom.
They show which way the energy travels. The arrow points from the thing eaten to the eater, because that is the direction the energy moves as food is eaten.

misconceptions.misconception: Dissolving is not a physical change.
misconceptions.overcome: Learners should recall how to separate salt and water from Stage 5. Explain that in most physical changes we can get back the substances we started with. The substances may look a bit different, but their particles have not changed in any way, except possibly in their arrangement. You can use the example of building blocks. We can arrange them in different ways to make structures that look different, but the actual blocks in each structure do not change.
learner: Dissolving must be a chemical change, because the solid seems to turn into something else.
It is a physical change. The particles of the solid are the same particles as before, just spread out among the water's. Nothing new was made, which is why evaporating the water gives the solid back.

misconceptions.misconception: Chemical reactions happen when you mix two substances, especially if the colour changes.
misconceptions.overcome: Point out that there is colour change because liquids of two different colours were mixed. The substances have not changed. Then do suggested Main activity 1.
learner: If you mix two things and the colour changes, a chemical reaction has happened.

Not by itself. Mix a red drink with a yellow one and you get orange, but both liquids are still there unchanged. A reaction means new substances have formed - so look for a gas being made, or a change in temperature, and not just a new colour.

misconceptions.misconception: Mass and weight mean the same thing and they are equal at all times.
misconceptions.overcome: This is a completely expected misconception because of the way we use the words 'weight' and 'weigh'. Read through What is the difference between mass and weight? in the Learner's Book.
learner: Mass and weight are two words for the same thing.

Mass is how much material something is made of, measured in kilograms. Weight is the pull of gravity on that mass, measured in newtons. Carry a 1 kg bag to the Moon and its mass is still 1 kg, while its weight falls to about a sixth.

misconceptions.misconception: If an object is stationary it has no forces acting on it.
misconceptions.overcome: Do question 3 in the Getting started activity - this shows gravity and normal forces acting on a ball at rest.
learner: If something is sitting still, no forces are acting on it.

There are usually two, and they balance. A ball resting on a table is pulled down by gravity and pushed up by the table with exactly as much force, so it stays put. Balanced is not the same as absent.

_supersedes: Where a row names `supersedes`, those extracted pairs are dropped from the unit's panel because the Cambridge row says the same thing better. Named rather than matched on word overlap: two fuzzy matchers were tried and both were wrong, one merging unrelated pairs on the word 'from' and the other missing 'The white cloud above a pot is water vapour' against 'The white cloud above a boiling kettle is the steam'. A named target that no longer exists fails the build, which is the point - the pack is re-extracted from Word documents and an override that quietly stops applying would leave the duplicate on the child's screen.
